sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Lyophyllum decastes often forms dense groups of mushrooms whose stems converge at the base. The smooth, fawn to grey-brown cap is usually 4–15 cm across; its margin starts inrolled and may become wavy. The crowded white to pale-grey gills are adnate. The stem is white and stout, sometimes slightly brown at the base. Solitary specimens also occur.

sections.title: Ecology and spores
sections.text: This saprotrophic species grows on humus-rich soil, woodland edges, paths and disturbed ground; it may be associated with buried, decaying wood. It fruits mainly from late summer into autumn. The spore print is white.

sections.title: Species complex
sections.text: Lyophyllum decastes in the broad sense includes closely related taxa that can be difficult to separate by visible characters alone. Colours, gill attachment and smell vary; a farinaceous smell is not a reliable character for the whole complex. The plate shows a typical combination, not a certain identification.

sections.title: Food use and caution
sections.text: The species is generally regarded as edible and appears on some positive mushroom lists, but digestive upsets are reported in some people and some guides advise against eating it. Eat only specimens identified with certainty by an expert. A published case of liver injury involved a dietary supplement and does not establish equivalent toxicity from an ordinary meal.

traits: Cap 4 to 15 cm, fawn to light brown, sometimes greyish, rolled wavy margin
White stout stem, often converging with other stems at the base; no ring
Humus-rich soil, woodland edges, paths or buried decaying wood · white spore print · late summer-autumn
safetyNote: Generally regarded as edible and included in positive lists, but digestive upsets are reported and some guides advise against eating it. The Lyophyllum decastes complex is difficult to identify; eat only specimens identified with certainty by an expert.
